justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline trajectory, with the 1-day estimate of 158.5 anchored closely to recent price action and short-term momentum. The 1-week estimate of 159.8 assumes continuation of the prevailing trend with minor drift upward, incorporating mean-reversion tendencies that prevent aggressive extrapolation. The 1-month estimate of 162.0 reflects a longer-run fundamental anchor — perhaps fair value modeling, earnings expectations, or macro backdrop — while acknowledging that over four weeks, compounding small positive drift produces a modestly higher target. Across all horizons, the point estimates are intentionally conservative, assuming no major catalysts in either direction and relatively stable market conditions.

The confidence interval widths widen appropriately as the forecast horizon extends. At one day, the 90% CI of roughly ±4.3 points reflects typical intraday-to-overnight volatility, which is relatively contained and driven primarily by market microstructure and overnight news flow. At one week, the interval expands to roughly ±9 points, capturing the possibility of scheduled economic releases, central bank communications, or sector-specific developments. At one month, the ±18-point interval reflects the full accumulation of uncertainty — earnings reports, geopolitical developments, changes in rate expectations, and liquidity conditions — all of which can compound meaningfully over that timeframe. Implied volatility derived from options markets, if available, would have directly informed these interval widths.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals in either direction. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a stronger-than-expected earnings report, an unexpected rate cut signal from a major central bank, or a resolution of a geopolitical overhang — could drive prices well above the 162–180 range even within a month. On the downside, a risk-off shock such as a credit event, a sharp deterioration in economic data, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions could push prices below the 144 lower bound of the 1-month interval. Liquidity conditions matter too — in thin markets, price moves can overshoot fair value significantly, making tail events more probable than a normal distribution assumption would suggest. My intervals attempt to be realistic rather than mechanically derived, but black swan events by definition fall outside any reasonably constructed forecast band.
